title: Nordic hamstring work protects hamstrings, and pairing it with plyometrics builds speed
citation: Sarraj, A.R. and Allaw, J. (2026). Eccentric vs. plyometric training for hamstring health in soccer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of injury prevention and athletic performance. Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-79351-y
tested: 54 randomized trials in soccer players aged 13 and older, comparing eccentric (Nordic hamstring) training, plyometric training, combined programs, and control groups.
finding: Eccentric Nordic training reduced hamstring injury incidence by approximately 70% (risk ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.48). Combined eccentric plus plyometric programs produced the largest sprint improvement (g = 1.02). Plyometrics alone improved sprint (g = 0.67). Eccentric training alone did not significantly improve sprint (g = 0.30).
key_number: About 70% lower hamstring injury incidence with Nordic training (risk ratio 0.29)
verdict_reason: The injury reduction is large and significant, and the sprint gain is real for combined programs. Eccentrics alone protect; the combination is what builds speed.
takeaway: Keep controlled Nordic hamstring work in the program for hamstring health, and pair it with plyometrics for speed. Build the workload gradually.
limits: The 70% injury figure rests on 4 of the 54 trials. The athletes were soccer players, not sprinters. The paper is an early-access accepted version published November 6, 2026 and may be edited before its final version.

title: Sled sprints help acceleration, but regular sprinting still matters
citation: Li, C., Chen, L. and Zhang, Q. (2025). Effects of resisted sprint training on sprint, jump, and change-of-direction performance in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology.
tested: 16 studies with 404 athletes, comparing resisted sprint training with unresisted sprinting and regular training.
finding: Resisted sprinting improved linear sprint performance (effect size 0.65) more than unresisted sprinting (0.42) within groups, but the head-to-head difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.057). Resisted training had a clear advantage for 0 to 10 m acceleration and for change of direction.
key_number: Effect size 0.65 for resisted vs 0.42 for unresisted sprinting; head-to-head difference not significant (p = 0.057)
verdict_reason: Both methods work. The resisted advantage is clear for the first 10 meters and change of direction, not for sprinting overall.
takeaway: Use sled accelerations to train the first few steps, and keep free sprints in the program so athletes practice moving fast without resistance.
limits: Effects vary with sled load and athlete level.

title: Plyometrics can improve 30-meter sprint times
citation: Effects of plyometric training on performance-related metrics in track and field athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (2026). PubMed Central.
tested: 30 randomized trials of plyometric training in track and field athletes.
finding: The pooled 30 m sprint result improved by 3.53% (p = 0.02). The 20 m result improved 1.23% but was not statistically significant (p = 0.11). Results varied substantially between studies.
verdict_reason: A significant pooled improvement at 30 m in the exact population this app serves, with honest variation between studies.
takeaway: Keep quality jumps, bounds and hops in the sprint program. Focus on clean contacts and controlled volume instead of doing more jumps just to get tired.
limits: The 20 m effect was not significant, and study results varied.

title: Flywheel training is not automatically better for sprint speed
citation: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Isoinertial Flywheel vs. Traditional Resistance Training on Strength, Power, Speed, and Agility in Team Sports (2026). PubMed.
tested: 13 studies, 324 team-sport athletes, flywheel vs conventional strength training (per Char, unverified).
finding: No significant difference for 10 m sprint (SMD -0.021, p = 0.206) or 20 m sprint (SMD -0.076, p = 0.132). Per Char, UNVERIFIED.
verdict_reason: Held. Luna's title search on 2026-11-06 did not surface this paper or its numbers, and other flywheel syntheses report different results. This entry stays draft until Luna opens the exact PubMed record and confirms the paper and figures.

title: A flywheel warm-up does not guarantee a faster sprint
citation: Acute effects of flywheel resistance training on jump and sprint performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis of inertial-load and rest-interval moderators (2026). BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation.
tested: 9 crossover trials measuring sprint and jump performance immediately after flywheel resistance exercise.
finding: No significant effect on sprint performance (SMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.22). Countermovement jump improved slightly (SMD 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.60), with the clearest effect 8 to 12 minutes after the exercise.
key_number: Sprint effect SMD -0.03 (no change); jump effect SMD 0.32
verdict_reason: A small acute jump benefit is real, but the sprint claim does not hold in the pooled data.
takeaway: Keep pre-sprint warm-ups simple and repeatable. Only add a flywheel activation exercise if your own timing data shows it helps the athlete.
limits: Evidence certainty was rated low by the authors.

title: More sleep was linked to faster sprint times
citation: Mah, C.D., Mah, K.E., Kezirian, E.J. and Dement, W.C. (2011). The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep, 34(7), 943-950. PubMed.
tested: Collegiate basketball players who extended their nightly sleep over several weeks while researchers tracked sleep and performance. No randomized control group.
finding: Nightly sleep increased by an average of 110.9 minutes. Mean 282-foot sprint time improved from 16.2 to 15.5 seconds (p < 0.001).
key_number: 0.7 seconds faster after about 111 extra minutes of sleep per night
verdict_reason: A clear improvement in the studied group, held back from a stronger claim only by the small, uncontrolled design.
takeaway: Treat sleep as part of training. Track sleep consistency alongside sprint times and daily readiness instead of looking only at workouts.
limits: Small study with no randomized control group; basketball players, not track athletes.

title: Sprinting once or twice a week can both improve speed
citation: Marzouki, H. et al. (2021). Effects of 1 vs. 2 sessions per week of equal-volume sprint training on explosive, high-intensity and endurance-intensive performances in young soccer players. Biology of Sport, 38, 175-183. PubMed Central.
tested: 36 male youth soccer players, about 17 years old, over 10 weeks. One group sprinted once per week, the other twice, with equal total sprint volume. Testing covered 10 m, 20 m, 30 m and flying 10 m.
finding: Both groups improved significantly (p < 0.001, effect size at least 0.80). There was no significant difference between groups for linear sprint performance (between-group effect size below 0.20).
key_number: Once vs twice per week at equal volume: no difference in sprint gains
verdict_reason: Frequency alone was not the lever at equal volume. Total quality work and recovery matter more than session count.
takeaway: Do not add speed sessions just to increase frequency. Plan quality sprint exposure around the total weekly workload and how well athletes recover.
limits: One study, youth soccer players; two sessions did help cardiorespiratory fitness more, which this entry does not cover.

title: Max-speed exposure matters, but the exact timing is not settled
citation: Buchheit, M. et al. (2023). Exposures to near-to-maximal speed running bouts during different turnarounds in elite football: association with match hamstring injuries. Biology of Sport, 40(4), 1057-1067. DOI: 10.5114/biolsport.2023.125595
tested: Training speed exposures and match hamstring injuries across 36 elite soccer team-seasons, 627 players and 96 non-contact match hamstring injuries. Observational study.
finding: In half of the turnarounds where players were exposed to running above 95% of their maximum speed in training, there were no match hamstring injuries at all, and no injuries occurred when that exposure fell two days before the match. The study is observational, so it cannot prove the exposure caused the lower injury counts.
key_number: Zero match hamstring injuries in half the weeks with above-95% speed exposure
verdict_reason: The association is consistent and the timing pattern is interesting, but an observational study in professional soccer cannot set a prescription for high school track.
takeaway: Track when athletes reach high speeds in training and build that exposure gradually. Do not copy a professional soccer match week directly into high school training.
limits: Observational; elite adult soccer players; exact exposure rates come from the full text and Luna verified the cohort, design and headline pattern against the published abstract.
